title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: What Is Information Retrieval (IR)
summary: Information Retrieval (IR) is the science of finding material — typically documents — that satisfies an information need from within large collections.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body:
Information Retrieval (IR) is the science of finding material — typically documents — that satisfies an information need from within large collections. The field covers the entire pipeline: representing documents, representing queries, computing relevance, ranking results, and evaluating quality. IR differs from database retrieval because it works with *unstructured* or *semi-structured* natural language text where exact match is insufficient. The core task is **ranking**: given a query q and corpus D, return a ranked list of documents ordered by estimated relevance. Modern IR underpins web search engines, enterprise search, question answering, and RAG systems.

```
Query q ──► [Query Representation]
                     │
                     ▼
Corpus D ──► [Document Representation]  ──► [Matching/Scoring] ──► [Ranked List]
```

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
IR SYSTEM PIPELINE
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

   OFFLINE (Index Time)
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Documents ──► Tokenise ──► Normalise ──► Index      │
   │                                            │          │
   │                              Inverted Index│          │
   │                         term → [doc1, doc3, doc7]    │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

   ONLINE (Query Time)
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Query ──► Tokenise ──► [Lookup in Index]            │
   │                                │                      │
   │                         Score(doc, query)             │
   │                         using retrieval model         │
   │                                │                      │
   │                         Rank  ──► Top-K Results       │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

RETRIEVAL MODEL COMPARISON
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Boolean   │ Exact match | AND/OR/NOT | No ranking
  TF-IDF    │ Weighted match | Cosine sim | Sparse vectors
  BM25      │ Probabilistic | TF-saturated | Length-norm
  LM (QL)   │ Query likelihood | Smoothed language model
  Dense     │ Semantic embeddings | ANN search | FAISS
```

quiz.explanation: (1) Indexing — building a data structure that enables fast lookup; (2) Retrieval — finding candidate documents matching the query; (3) Ranking — ordering candidates by estimated relevance.

quiz.question: What distinguishes IR from database querying?
options: (1) Vocabulary mismatch (no synonym handling). (2) All common terms get low IDF — the model degrades on queries with only high-frequency terms.
Parse into a query tree. Evaluate bottom-up.
Email filters, database full-text search (MySQL MATCH IN BOOLEAN MODE), legal/patent search (professionals want precise control), Elasticsearch filter context (exact,…
Databases retrieve exact matches on structured data with SQL.
quiz.explanation: Databases retrieve exact matches on structured data with SQL. IR deals with approximate relevance matching on unstructured text. IR tolerates ambiguity; databases do not.

quiz.question: Define the ad-hoc retrieval task.
options: An evaluation methodology pioneered at Cranfield University.
An inverted index maps each unique term to a list (posting list) of document IDs where that term appears, with optional frequency and position data.
/n or NEAR(n) — requires two terms to appear within n positions of each other.
The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
quiz.explanation: Given a static document collection and a new query, retrieve the most relevant documents. The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies. This is the standard TREC evaluation setting.

quiz.question: What is an information need vs a query?
options: Documents outside the pool are assumed non-relevant (a known bias for systems that retrieve from outside the pool).
An extension of the LM framework for query expansion. Take top-K retrieved documents, estimate a relevance model P(t|R) from them, interpolate with the original query model, and re-retrieve.
An evaluation methodology pioneered at Cranfield University.
An information need is the underlying intent ("I want to understand BM25 tuning").
quiz.explanation: An information need is the underlying intent ("I want to understand BM25 tuning"). A query is the user's linguistic expression of that need ("BM25 k1 b parameters"). They often don't match perfectly — bridging this gap is a core IR challenge.

quiz.question: What is the vocabulary mismatch problem?
options: The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
New York" ≠ {"New", "York"} semantically. BoW matches documents with "New" and "York" anywhere, not necessarily adjacent.
Either TF=0 (term doesn't appear in the document) or IDF=0 (term appears in every document and is thus useless for discrimination).
The query uses different words than the document. E.g., query = "heart attack", document = "myocardial infarction".
quiz.explanation: The query uses different words than the document. E.g., query = "heart attack", document = "myocardial infarction". Lexical models (BM25, TF-IDF) fail because they require exact token overlap.
